package_info.package_manager: Unix package managers (Debian, Fedora, openSUSE, Arch, Kali, macOS Homebrew, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: A backdoor was intentionally introduced by a trusted maintainer, allowing attackers to inject malicious code into OpenSSH server processes, bypass authentication, and execute arbitrary payloads. The backdoor was present in official releases, making it a high-impact supply chain compromise.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when OpenSSH server starts and loads liblzma from XZ Utils)
execution_context.file_location: liblzma (XZ Utils library, distributed in package tarballs and system packages)
required_permissions: network (for potential C2 or payload delivery)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Obfuscated code in liblzma that hooks into OpenSSH server process, intercepts authentication routines, and allows bypass or arbitrary code execution. (Exact code not shown in article, but described as a backdoor in the compression library.)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code hooks into the OpenSSH server process via the malicious liblzma library, intercepts authentication routines, and allows attackers to bypass password-based authentication or execute arbitrary payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is intentionally obfuscated, hooks into a critical authentication process, and enables unauthorized access or code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal compression libraries should not interact with authentication routines or enable code execution in unrelated processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Compression libraries may use hooks for performance or debugging, but never for authentication bypass or arbitrary code execution.
key_indicators: Obfuscated code in a widely used library
Enables authentication bypass and arbitrary code execution
Introduced by a trusted maintainer with elevated privileges

attack_chain.action: Malicious maintainer introduces obfuscated backdoor code into XZ Utils (liblzma) and publishes new package versions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Distribution of malicious package to downstream OS distributions.

attack_chain.action: Operating system vendors (Debian, Fedora, etc.) package and distribute the new XZ Utils versions in beta/unstable releases.
attack_chain.leads_to: Deployment of malicious library on user systems.

attack_chain.action: When OpenSSH server starts, it loads the malicious liblzma library.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor code executes in the context of the OpenSSH server.

attack_chain.action: Backdoor code intercepts authentication routines, allowing attackers to bypass authentication or execute arbitrary payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Unauthorized access or remote code execution on affected systems (final goal).

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated or non-standard code in core libraries (liblzma, compression utilities)
Unexpected hooks or function overrides in authentication processes
Compression library code paths that interact with network or authentication subsystems
file_indicators: liblzma.so or liblzma.dylib with unexpected code sections or hashes
Unusual changes in XZ Utils source code repository
network_indicators: Unexpected outbound connections from OpenSSH server process
C2 domains or IPs contacted by OpenSSH or liblzma
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for installation of XZ Utils versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1, especially in beta or unstable OS releases. Perform static and dynamic analysis of liblzma to detect obfuscated code or unexpected hooks into authentication routines. Monitor OpenSSH server processes for abnormal behavior, such as authentication bypass or unexpected network activity. Compare library hashes against known-good versions and audit source code changes for suspicious commits.
